title: Refuge before the righteous Judge.
intro: Seventeen verses move from pursuit and an appeal for a fair hearing through self-examination, judgment, and the consequences of evil, ending in praise.
context: The heading calls this a Shiggaion of David concerning the words of Cush, a Benjamite. The chapter does not explain the musical term, identify Cush further, or narrate the dispute. Its prayer moves from refuge through a conditional declaration about the speaker’s conduct to a wider appeal for righteous judgment. Images of weapons, childbirth, and a pit give the warning its force; the last verse turns to thanksgiving.
peopleNote: David is named in the heading. Cush is named as a Benjamite, but the chapter supplies no biography or quoted accusation; do not identify him with another biblical Cush or invent an encounter. David’s existing profile can provide related stories without presenting them as this psalm’s setting. All planned people and places in the paintings are imagined.

verses.title: A refuge amid pursuit
verses.heading: The first appeal is for rescue
verses.meaning: The speaker addresses the LORD as his God and takes refuge in Him while asking for deliverance from pursuers. Trust and an urgent need for help stand together at the beginning. The prayer does not require danger to be minimized before it can be spoken. It invites a reader to name a need for protection, bring it before God, and receive practical support while seeking safety. Refuge is the speaker’s act of reliance within an unresolved situation.
verses.contextTitle: The heading names a dispute without telling its story
verses.context: The source heading names David and the words of Cush, a Benjamite, but gives no further account of the conflict. Verse 2 completes the opening plea with a lion image. Preserve the heading as the bundled BSB carries it, without supplying a biography for Cush.
explore: I take refuge in You
The opening places the speaker’s hope in the LORD while a threat remains. It is a prayer from within danger.
All my pursuers
The request is broad, but the text does not enumerate the people involved. A sheltered traveler in the planned art remains anonymous.
verses.reflect: Where do you need shelter or support today? What could you name in prayer, and who could help you take a practical step toward safety?
verses.alt: An imagined ancient traveler rests beneath a rocky overhang above an olive valley as distant figures remain far down the path.
verses.scene: An anonymous ancient traveler pauses under a broad rocky overhang at the edge of an olive valley, small distant figures far down a winding path, sober early light, shelter amid pursuit without a confrontation.

verses.title: The threat pictured as a lion
verses.heading: A fierce image gives danger its weight
verses.meaning: The speaker compares the destructive threat to a lion tearing prey, then names the fear that no rescuer will be there. This is intense poetic language for vulnerability and danger. It belongs to the appeal for deliverance begun in verse 1, rather than a separate account of an animal attack. The verse lets fear be expressed plainly. A reader can acknowledge the seriousness of a threat without treating the painting or the comparison as evidence about a specific event.
verses.contextTitle: The comparison completes the opening request
verses.context: Verse 2 follows directly from the plea to be saved from pursuers. The poem then turns in verses 3–5 toward the speaker’s own conduct. Keep the lion comparison within that opening plea rather than attaching an invented incident from David’s life.
explore: Like a lion
The comparison makes destructive pursuit vivid. It does not identify an actual animal present in the dispute.
No one to rescue me
The feared lack of help intensifies the plea. The planned painting suggests distance and vulnerability without showing an attack.
verses.reflect: What fear feels especially hard to say aloud? Who could hear it without dismissing it or leaving you to carry it alone?
verses.alt: A distant lion stands on a rocky ridge across a deep valley while an anonymous traveler remains in shelter in the foreground.
verses.scene: A distant lion silhouetted on a rocky ridge across a wide olive valley, an anonymous traveler sheltered in the foreground, a clear sense of separation and vulnerability, no pursuit or attack, no blood.

verses.title: Bring my own conduct into the light
verses.heading: The speaker begins a conditional appeal
verses.meaning: The speaker asks God to consider whether he has done the wrong at issue and whether injustice is on his hands. The repeated conditional wording opens a declaration that continues through verse 5. He brings his own conduct under scrutiny while asking for help against others. That order invites an honest response to conflict: seek a fair hearing, and be willing to examine your part. The verse does not disclose the full accusation or give the reader enough detail to reconstruct the case.
verses.contextTitle: Do not stop the sentence before verse 5
verses.context: Verses 3–4 set out conditions, and verse 5 supplies the consequence the speaker invokes if those conditions are true. Read them as a connected appeal. The words “done this” point toward a dispute whose complete details are not preserved here.
explore: If I have done this
The conditional wording matters. The speaker is not confessing the described act in this sentence.
Injustice is on my hands
Hands give conduct a concrete image. Open, empty hands in the planned watercolor symbolize willingness to be examined.
verses.reflect: Is there a part of a disagreement that you need to examine honestly? What would it look like to seek truth about your own actions as well as another person’s?
verses.alt: An ancient traveler sits beside a clear stream, looking at open hands in quiet self-examination.
verses.scene: An anonymous ancient traveler sits beside a clear shallow stream beneath olive branches, open empty hands held thoughtfully over the water, reflective morning light, no washing ritual or claim of historical reconstruction.

verses.title: Integrity toward ally and foe
verses.heading: The appeal names conduct across a conflict
verses.meaning: The speaker continues the conditional statement by naming harm toward an ally and unjust plundering of a foe. The appeal concerns how he has treated people on both sides of a relationship. The presence of an enemy does not make every action toward that person just. Read this verse with the sentence it belongs to, then consider its searching question: do loyalty and opposition change how fairly we behave? The speaker’s particular dispute remains undescribed beyond the terms supplied in the poem.
verses.contextTitle: The conditional list continues from verse 3
verses.context: The BSB wording names an ally and a foe without cause for plundering. Verse 5 completes the declaration. Avoid converting the conditional list into a narrated episode or identifying the ally and foe as named people absent from these verses.
explore: My ally
The verse includes obligations toward someone at peace with the speaker. Trust is part of what conduct can protect or damage.
My foe without cause
The line brings restraint toward an opponent into the appeal. The planned shared path symbolizes ethical choices, not an actual meeting.
verses.reflect: Do you apply a different standard of fairness to someone you dislike? What honest or restrained action could you choose in a difficult relationship?
verses.alt: Two anonymous travelers pass at a respectful distance on an ancient hillside path, with unclaimed goods resting beside a wall.
verses.scene: Two anonymous ancient travelers pass at a respectful distance on a narrow olive hillside path, a modest pack of goods beside a low wall, hands unthreatening, sober respectful mood, no theft depicted.

verses.title: The solemn weight of the appeal
verses.heading: A conditional consequence completes the declaration
verses.meaning: The speaker invokes pursuit, defeat, and the loss of honor if the wrong described in verses 3–4 is truly his. This is a solemn way of placing his claim before God. It should be read as the consequence of that conditional declaration, rather than an instruction for a distressed reader to wish harm upon themselves. The language shows how seriously the speaker takes his appeal to integrity. Selah remains part of the source, allowing its place in the poem to be seen without an invented translation.
verses.contextTitle: The consequence belongs to the preceding conditions
verses.context: Read verse 5 immediately after verses 3–4. The next verse returns to an appeal for God to act against the enemies’ fury. The text describes what the speaker invokes conditionally; it does not narrate a defeat that has occurred.
explore: Then may my enemy
The word “then” completes the conditional movement. Separating the verse from its beginning changes its function.
Honor in the dust
The image makes disgrace tangible. A fallen cloak on the planned path symbolizes lost honor without depicting a person being trampled.
verses.reflect: What would accountability look like in a conflict you are facing? Is there a truthful conversation or an act of repair that belongs to you?
verses.alt: A travel cloak lies on a dusty ancient path beside an upright staff, with no injured person present.
verses.scene: A simple travel cloak fallen onto a dusty ancient path beside an upright walking staff and olive roots, restrained quiet light, symbolic loss of honor, no body, injury or trampling.

verses.title: Arise and ordain judgment
verses.heading: The prayer asks God to answer the enemies’ fury
verses.meaning: The speaker asks the LORD to arise in anger and ordain judgment. The strong appeal answers the fury he attributes to his enemies. It is a request that God act as judge, with wrong treated seriously. The language of waking gives urgency to the prayer without requiring a literal account of God sleeping. Read it as an appeal for divine action. It offers words for seeking justice while leaving judgment with God rather than claiming authority for personal retaliation.
verses.contextTitle: The prayer returns from self-examination to action
verses.context: After the conditional appeal of verses 3–5, verse 6 asks for judgment. Verse 7 widens the scene to assembled peoples. The change in imagery belongs to the poem’s movement toward a judicial hearing, not a narrated battle.
explore: Arise, O LORD
The imperative voices urgent dependence. The speaker is asking God to act, rather than describing an action already witnessed.
Ordain judgment
The appeal seeks an ordered judgment against fury. The planned clearing sky symbolizes that hope without portraying God.
verses.reflect: What wrong do you need to bring before God clearly? What appropriate help could support a just response without turning it into personal revenge?
verses.alt: Heavy clouds part above a broad ancient gathering place as a lone petitioner waits below.
verses.scene: A broad empty ancient stone gathering place beneath heavy clouds opening to clear light, a small anonymous petitioner at the edge, solemn expectation of justice, no divine figure or face-shaped clouds.

verses.title: A hearing larger than one person
verses.heading: The assembled peoples gather before the Judge
verses.meaning: The speaker’s appeal now pictures peoples gathered around God and asks Him to take His seat on high. The scale expands beyond the individual who began by fleeing pursuers. Judicial authority and a gathering of people give the request for justice a public dimension. The poem does not name the peoples, describe their faces, or locate a physical throne. The verse invites a reader to see personal grievances within a larger concern for justice that reaches other people as well.
verses.contextTitle: The gathering leads into judgment of the peoples
verses.context: Verse 7 follows the request to ordain judgment and prepares for verse 8’s statement that the LORD judges the peoples. Read the elevated seat as part of the poem’s judicial imagery. No specific earthly assembly or dated event is identified.
explore: The assembled peoples
The plural widens the field of view beyond the original dispute. It gives no list of nations or groups to add.
Take Your seat on high
The image expresses authority over the assembly. The planned art will suggest a gathering without painting a visible divine ruler.
verses.reflect: Who else is affected by a situation you are praying about? How could your hope for justice include their needs too?
verses.alt: Small groups of anonymous ancient people gather in a wide natural stone amphitheater beneath an open sky.
verses.scene: Small groups of anonymous ancient people gather in a wide natural stone amphitheater among olive hills, immense open luminous sky, solemn public hearing suggested, no throne, divine person or identifiable historical event.

verses.title: A plea for vindication
verses.heading: The speaker submits his claim to the LORD’s judgment
verses.meaning: The verse joins a statement about the LORD judging peoples with a personal request for vindication according to righteousness and integrity. Read within the earlier conditional appeal, the speaker presents his conduct in the dispute for a fair verdict. The line need not be stretched into a claim that he has never done wrong in his life. It brings his case before the judge he trusts. A response can seek truthful vindication while remaining willing for one’s own account to be examined.
verses.contextTitle: The personal request remains within a wider judgment
verses.context: Verse 7 pictures gathered peoples; verse 8 names the LORD as their judge and returns to the speaker’s case. Verses 3–5 explain the solemn willingness to be judged that accompanies his appeal. Verse 9 then asks for evil to end.
explore: Vindicate me
The request seeks a right verdict. It does not itself provide the reader with all the facts of the dispute.
Righteousness and integrity
These words belong to the speaker’s appeal before God. The planned steady posture symbolizes an honest hearing without depicting a guaranteed victory.
verses.reflect: Where do you need a fair hearing? What would help you present the truth carefully and remain open to correction?
verses.alt: An anonymous ancient petitioner stands with open hands in a quiet stone courtyard, awaiting a fair hearing.
verses.scene: An anonymous ancient petitioner stands with open hands in a simple quiet stone courtyard, attentive figures far behind, level morning light, dignified hope for a fair hearing, no literal divine judge.

verses.title: The God who searches within
verses.heading: The appeal reaches beyond outward appearances
verses.meaning: The prayer asks for an end to the wicked person’s evil and for the righteous to be established. It addresses God as the One who searches hearts and minds. In this appeal, justice is concerned with more than the appearance of a case: inward motives also lie within God’s knowledge. The line can encourage hope that hidden wrong matters, and invite honest examination of our own intentions. It asks for evil to end without giving the reader permission to assume complete knowledge of another person’s heart.
verses.contextTitle: A shared appeal follows the personal request
verses.context: Verse 8 asks for personal vindication; verse 9 broadens the prayer toward the end of evil and the establishing of the righteous. Preserve the BSB wording about hearts and minds without adding unsupported explanations of ancient anatomy.
explore: Put an end to the evil
The request focuses the hope of judgment on evil losing its hold. It remains a petition addressed to God.
Searches hearts and minds
The inward image can turn a reader toward self-examination as well as confidence in a just hearing. The planned clear water is symbolic.
verses.reflect: What intention behind your actions needs honest attention? What change would help you seek what is right with a clearer heart?
verses.alt: A quiet pool reflects olive branches and an open sky while an ancient traveler sits in thoughtful stillness nearby.
verses.scene: A clear still pool reflecting olive branches and an open sky, an anonymous ancient traveler quietly considering the reflection from a nearby rock, contemplative honest mood, no literal exposed heart or anatomy.

verses.title: My shield is with God
verses.heading: The speaker names the source of his defense
verses.meaning: The speaker places his shield with God and speaks of God saving the upright in heart. The protective image follows the appeal to the God who searches inwardly, connecting defense with the integrity at issue throughout the prayer. The verse expresses reliance in the middle of a conflict whose outcome has not been narrated. It can become a prayer for protection while leaving room for practical help and wise boundaries. The shield image does not require a promise that faithful people will never suffer harm.
verses.contextTitle: The language of the heart continues from verse 9
verses.context: The God who searches hearts and minds in verse 9 is described as saving the upright in heart in verse 10. Verse 11 will name Him a righteous judge. The shield links protection with the judicial confidence of the surrounding lines.
explore: My shield
An ordinary defensive object gives trust a visible image. The planned shield remains symbolic rather than an artifact attributed to David.
Upright in heart
The wording keeps inward integrity in view. Read it beside the appeal to be searched rather than as a means of judging another person’s hidden motives.
verses.reflect: What source of support helps you stand steadily in a conflict? What protection or help could you ask for today?
verses.alt: A worn round shield rests beside an anonymous traveler beneath an olive tree overlooking a quiet valley.
verses.scene: A worn simple round shield rests beside an anonymous ancient traveler under a broad olive tree, quiet valley and restrained morning light, protective trust without triumphant display or visible divinity.

verses.title: Justice that takes wrong seriously
verses.heading: Righteous judgment includes indignation
verses.meaning: The verse names God as a righteous judge and speaks of His indignation each day. The poem does not present justice as indifference toward wrong. Its severe language belongs to the speaker’s confidence that evil matters before God. It should remain audible alongside the earlier need for rescue and the coming warning about repentance. The reader can ask how to care about injustice without letting anger become a claim to God’s authority or a reason to act cruelly toward another person.
verses.contextTitle: The confession prepares for the weapon imagery
verses.context: Verse 11 follows the shield and precedes the conditional warning of verses 12–13. The movement holds protection and judgment together. The poem supplies no calendar of punishments or narrated event corresponding to the phrase about each day.
explore: A righteous judge
The line locates the character of judgment in righteousness. It supports the appeal for a fair hearing developed earlier.
Indignation each day
The phrase expresses sustained opposition to wrong. The planned storm-lit landscape suggests seriousness without picturing a divine face or human retaliation.
verses.reflect: What injustice needs your careful attention? How could your response remain truthful and proportionate while you seek what is right?
verses.alt: An ancient stone gate stands beneath a storm-lit sky, with a clear path leading through it toward olive hills.
verses.scene: An old simple stone gate beneath a sober storm-lit sky, clear unblocked path through the gate toward olive hills, restrained solemn light, righteous judgment suggested symbolically, no divine face or punitive spectacle.

verses.title: The warning calls for turning
verses.heading: Repentance stands at the beginning of the warning
verses.meaning: The verse opens with the condition that a person does not repent, then pictures God sharpening a sword and preparing a bow. The condition matters: the warning concerns persistence in wrongdoing. Martial imagery gives the prospect of judgment force. It is not a task assigned to the reader to carry out with weapons. The line can invite a concrete response to correction now: recognize wrong, turn from it, and take responsibility while there is an opportunity to do so.
verses.contextTitle: Keep the condition with the weapons
verses.context: Verse 12 begins a warning that continues in verse 13. The sword and bow belong to poetic language about divine judgment, after the confession that God is a righteous judge. The chapter does not describe a physical weapon used in a narrated encounter.
explore: If one does not repent
The condition makes turning from wrong part of the warning. Do not omit it when explaining the verse.
Sword and bow
The weapon images make judgment formidable. The planned still life will show the objects without a wielder or an act of violence.
verses.reflect: Is there a correction you have been postponing? What small, specific act could begin a change of direction today?
verses.alt: An ancient sword, bow, and whetstone lie on a stone ledge with no person holding them.
verses.scene: A simple ancient sword beside a whetstone and a strung wooden bow resting on a stone ledge, sober cool olive-hill background, no wielder, aimed weapon, blood, injury or divine figure.

verses.title: The seriousness of judgment
verses.heading: The weapon imagery continues
verses.meaning: The poem continues its severe description of prepared weapons and arrows with fire. Read with verse 12, the image warns about wrongdoing that refuses to turn. The force of the language should not be removed, but its literary role should stay clear: this is a warning in a prayer about God’s judgment. It gives no instructions for human violence. The following verses turn from the divine-warrior image toward ways that evil brings trouble back upon the one who practices it.
verses.contextTitle: The warning leads into another set of images
verses.context: Verse 13 completes the weapon language begun after the condition about repentance. Verse 14 shifts to conception and birth, followed by a pit and recoiling trouble. These changes are poetic images, not scenes in a single literal battle story.
explore: Prepared His deadly weapons
The statement stresses readiness for judgment. Keep it beside the condition in the preceding verse.
Arrows with fire
The vivid image makes the warning severe. The planned art shows an unhandled arrow and a small controlled flame without depicting an attack.
verses.reflect: What helps you take the consequences of a choice seriously before you act? Is there a harmful course you can stop or seek help to change?
verses.alt: An ancient quiver and unhandled arrows rest on stone beside a small controlled brazier, with no person or target nearby.
verses.scene: An ancient quiver and several unhandled arrows on a stone surface beside a small controlled brazier, solemn restrained light, symbolic warning of judgment, no targets, attack, injury, bodies or divine figure.

verses.title: How wrongdoing grows
verses.heading: Conception and birth become images for evil
verses.meaning: The verse uses the process of conceiving, laboring, and giving birth as a metaphor for evil, trouble, and falsehood coming into the world. Its subject is a wicked person’s developing wrongdoing. It is not a statement that pregnancy or a mother’s body is evil. The image makes the movement from inward intention to outward result vivid. A reader can ask what is being allowed to grow in thought, speech, or plans, and choose to interrupt something harmful before it is acted out.
verses.contextTitle: A new metaphor follows the weapons
verses.context: Verse 14 changes the imagery from judgment’s weapons to the development of wrongdoing. Verses 15–16 then describe a trap and trouble returning to its maker. Keep these as linked poetic observations rather than an invented biography of an enemy.
explore: Conceives trouble
The metaphor begins before the outward result. It can direct attention toward intentions and plans.
Births falsehood
Falsehood is the result named in the image. The planned tangled vines are an explicitly symbolic response that avoids presenting pregnancy as a moral defect.
verses.reflect: What thought or plan have you been feeding that could lead to harm? What healthier action could interrupt its growth?
verses.alt: Tangled vines grow around an abandoned workbench on an ancient hillside, while a clear path remains open beyond.
verses.scene: Tangled thorny vines growing around an abandoned simple workbench and unfinished wooden framework on an olive hillside, a clear path beyond, symbolic harmful plans growing into trouble, no pregnancy, infants or bodily imagery.

verses.title: The maker falls into the pit
verses.heading: A trap becomes an image of reversal
verses.meaning: The person who digs and hollows out a pit falls into the place he has made. The poem makes wrongdoing’s reversal concrete: a device meant for another person becomes its maker’s undoing. Read it as the psalm’s image of just consequence. It does not teach that every accident or hardship proves someone has secretly done wrong, or that people can always see justice happen immediately. The verse invites a reader to abandon harmful schemes and consider what their own choices are making possible.
verses.contextTitle: The pit gives the next verse its shape
verses.context: Verse 15 supplies a concrete picture; verse 16 speaks more directly of trouble recoiling and violence returning. Together they describe a reversal within the psalm’s confidence in judgment. No named person or dated incident of falling into a hole is narrated.
explore: He has dug a hole
The person is responsible for making the trap. That responsibility is essential to the image.
A pit of his own making
The intended direction of harm turns back. The planned art uses an empty pit and abandoned tools without showing a person injured.
verses.reflect: Are you investing energy in something that could harm another person and yourself? What would it mean to stop building that trap?
verses.alt: An empty freshly dug pit and abandoned digging tools lie beside a rocky ancient path, with no injured person shown.
verses.scene: An empty freshly dug pit beside an ancient rocky path, abandoned wooden-handled digging tools, loosened soil, sober olive-grove setting, no trapped person, injury or body.

verses.title: Trouble returns to its source
verses.heading: The poem names the recoil of violence
verses.meaning: The speaker describes trouble recoiling on the wrongdoer and violence falling upon its source. This expresses the hope that wrongdoing will not keep its advantage. The line gives the pit image of verse 15 a direct moral conclusion. It belongs to a poem that appeals to God for judgment, rather than a command to make another person suffer. A response can seek an end to harm while refusing retaliation, and can acknowledge that the timing and shape of justice are not supplied here.
verses.contextTitle: The reversal closes before the turn to praise
verses.context: Verses 14–16 move through conceived trouble, a self-made pit, and violence returning. Verse 17 then changes from describing the wicked person to the speaker’s own promise of thanksgiving. Preserve that change of focus in the study.
explore: His trouble recoils
The language turns a harmful intention back toward its origin. It voices a moral reversal within the psalm.
His violence
The wrong belongs to the person described. The reader is not commissioned to carry out a violent response.
verses.reflect: What would help you seek an end to harm without adding harm of your own? Who could support a fair and peaceful next step?
verses.alt: A collapsed wooden snare lies tangled in its own cord beside an ancient path under a clearing sky.
verses.scene: A collapsed wooden snare tangled in its own cord beside an ancient olive hillside path, clearing sky, sober image of a harmful device failing, no animal, person, injury or triumphant mockery.

verses.title: The last word is thanksgiving
verses.heading: The speaker turns toward praise for God’s righteousness
verses.meaning: The final verse is the speaker’s commitment to thank the LORD for His righteousness and sing praise to His name as Most High. The opening sought refuge from pursuers; the ending gives the speaker a response shaped by the character of the God he has addressed. No completed rescue scene is narrated between those lines. The verse can invite gratitude and worship alongside an unresolved appeal for justice, without demanding that a distressed person pretend the pain has vanished.
verses.contextTitle: The promise of praise completes the poem
verses.context: Verse 17 follows the images of evil turning back on its maker. The speaker’s focus now returns explicitly to the LORD’s righteousness. Read the ending alongside verse 1 to hear the movement from asking for refuge to expressing thanksgiving.
explore: For His righteousness
The reason for praise is the character emphasized throughout the appeal for judgment.
I will thank … and sing
The speaker names his intended response. The planned musician is an anonymous expression of praise, not a portrait of David or a claim that a historical performance has been reconstructed.
verses.reflect: What can you thank God for while a difficult situation remains unfinished? What form of praise would feel honest today?
verses.alt: An anonymous ancient musician sits with a simple lyre beneath an olive tree overlooking hills in restrained evening light.
verses.scene: An anonymous ancient musician with a simple lyre beneath an olive tree, wide valley in restrained warm evening light, thoughtful gratitude with signs of a long journey, no crown, labels, portrait claim or visible divinity.
